sections.collegeNotes:
**Main organs.** The male system centers on the **testes** (the male gonads), plus a duct system and glands:

- **Testes:** produce **sperm** and the hormone **testosterone**. They sit outside the body in the **scrotum**, which keeps them slightly cooler than core temperature — necessary for sperm production.
- **Duct system:** sperm travel from the testes through the **epididymis** (where they mature and are stored), then the **ductus (vas) deferens**, and out through the **urethra** (which in males carries both urine and semen, at different times).
- **Accessory glands:** the **seminal vesicles, prostate gland, and bulbourethral glands** add fluids that nourish and transport sperm, forming **semen**.
- **Penis:** delivers semen.

**Spermatogenesis.** **Sperm production (spermatogenesis)** occurs continuously in the testes from puberty onward, producing huge numbers of sperm. It involves a special cell division (**meiosis**) that halves the chromosome number, so each sperm carries **23 chromosomes** (half a set) — so that fertilization restores the full 46. Each sperm is streamlined for its job: a **head** with genetic material (and enzymes to penetrate the egg), a **midpiece** packed with mitochondria for energy, and a **tail (flagellum)** for swimming.

**Testosterone.** The testes produce **testosterone**, the main male sex hormone (an androgen — a lipid-soluble steroid). It drives **sperm production**, the development of male **secondary sexual characteristics** (deeper voice, facial and body hair, muscle growth) at puberty, and libido. Testosterone is regulated by the **hypothalamus–pituitary** axis (recall FSH and LH from the endocrine unit): LH stimulates testosterone production, and FSH supports sperm production, with negative feedback keeping levels in range.

**The sperm's path.** Putting it together, sperm follow a clear route:

```
Testes (made) → epididymis (mature/stored) → ductus deferens → (join gland fluids = semen) → urethra → out
```

This pathway, plus hormonal control, is the framework for understanding male fertility and related clinical topics.

sections.eli10:
### ELI-10 Explains

### Simple idea
The male reproductive system makes sperm and the hormone testosterone, and it has a set of tubes and glands that prepare and deliver the sperm.

### Analogy
Think of it like a specialized factory with a delivery route. The **testes** are the factories that make two products: tiny swimmers (**sperm**) and a powerful chemical messenger (**testosterone**). The sperm aren't ready right away — they first spend time in a "training and storage" area (the **epididymis**) to mature. When it's time, they travel through a delivery tube (the **ductus deferens**), pick up nourishing fluids from **glands** along the way (making **semen**), and exit through the shared exit pipe (the **urethra**). The whole factory is kept slightly cooler than the rest of the body (in the **scrotum**) because sperm production doesn't work well when it's too warm.

### What is actually happening
**Testosterone** is the hormone that, at puberty, brings the deeper voice, facial hair, and muscle growth, and it keeps sperm production going — all controlled by "boss" hormones (**LH** and **FSH**) from the pituitary, just like other glands. Each sperm carries only **half** a set of genetic instructions (**23 chromosomes**), so that when it meets an egg (which also has half), they combine to make a complete set of 46. Understanding this system helps explain **fertility** issues and common conditions like an enlarged **prostate**, which sits around the urethra and can make urination difficult.

### Where the analogy stops
A factory makes a fixed number of items, but the testes churn out enormous numbers of sperm continuously, day after day, from puberty onward — far more than any single delivery uses.

sourceSnapshotMarkdown:
# Male Reproductive System

## What This Topic Is

This section covers the **male reproductive system**: the **testes**, the duct system, accessory glands, and how **sperm** and **testosterone** are produced and regulated.

## Why It Matters

The male reproductive system produces sperm and hormones essential for reproduction and secondary sexual characteristics. Understanding it supports care in fertility, hormonal health, and related conditions.

## Learning Objectives

- Identify the major **male reproductive organs**.
- Explain **sperm production (spermatogenesis)**.
- Describe **testosterone** and its effects.
- Describe the pathway sperm travel.

## Core Explanation

**Main organs.** The male system centers on the **testes** (the male gonads), plus a duct system and glands:

- **Testes:** produce **sperm** and the hormone **testosterone**. They sit outside the body in the **scrotum**, which keeps them slightly cooler than core temperature — necessary for sperm production.
- **Duct system:** sperm travel from the testes through the **epididymis** (where they mature and are stored), then the **ductus (vas) deferens**, and out through the **urethra** (which in males carries both urine and semen, at different times).
- **Accessory glands:** the **seminal vesicles, prostate gland, and bulbourethral glands** add fluids that nourish and transport sperm, forming **semen**.
- **Penis:** delivers semen.

**Spermatogenesis.** **Sperm production (spermatogenesis)** occurs continuously in the testes from puberty onward, producing huge numbers of sperm. It involves a special cell division (**meiosis**) that halves the chromosome number, so each sperm carries **23 chromosomes** (half a set) — so that fertilization restores the full 46. Each sperm is streamlined for its job: a **head** with genetic material (and enzymes to penetrate the egg), a **midpiece** packed with mitochondria for energy, and a **tail (flagellum)** for swimming.

**Testosterone.** The testes produce **testosterone**, the main male sex hormone (an androgen — a lipid-soluble steroid). It drives **sperm production**, the development of male **secondary sexual characteristics** (deeper voice, facial and body hair, muscle growth) at puberty, and libido. Testosterone is regulated by the **hypothalamus–pituitary** axis (recall FSH and LH from the endocrine unit): LH stimulates testosterone production, and FSH supports sperm production, with negative feedback keeping levels in range.

**The sperm's path.** Putting it together, sperm follow a clear route:

```
Testes (made) → epididymis (mature/stored) → ductus deferens → (join gland fluids = semen) → urethra → out
```

This pathway, plus hormonal control, is the framework for understanding male fertility and related clinical topics.

## How It Works

Production and regulation:

```
Hypothalamus → pituitary (LH, FSH) → testes
   LH → testosterone (sperm production, male characteristics, libido)
   FSH → supports spermatogenesis
Negative feedback keeps hormone levels balanced
Sperm: testes → epididymis → ductus deferens → urethra (as semen)
```

## Important Relationships and Comparisons

| Structure | Function |
| --- | --- |
| Testes | Make sperm + testosterone |
| Epididymis | Sperm maturation/storage |
| Ductus deferens | Carries sperm |
| Accessory glands | Add fluid → semen |
| Urethra | Carries semen (and urine) out |

| Hormone | Source | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Testosterone | Testes | Sperm, male characteristics, libido |
| LH | Pituitary | Stimulates testosterone |
| FSH | Pituitary | Supports sperm production |

## High-Yield Pre-Nursing Connections

Understanding this system supports care in **male infertility** (sperm production/quality), **hormonal disorders** (low testosterone), and conditions like **benign prostatic hyperplasia** (enlarged prostate affecting urination — note the prostate surrounds the urethra) and prostate cancer. The temperature sensitivity of sperm production and the hormonal axis are relevant to fertility. Because the male urethra carries both urine and semen, urinary and reproductive health overlap.

## Common Confusions

- **Testes make both sperm and testosterone.**
- **Sperm mature in the epididymis**, not in the testes alone.
- **Sperm carry 23 chromosomes** (half), restored to 46 at fertilization.
- **The male urethra is shared** by the urinary and reproductive systems.

## Memory Aids

- **Sperm path: "Testes, Epididymis, Ductus (vas) deferens, Urethra" — "TEDU."**
- **Testosterone = "the male-characteristics + sperm hormone."**
- **Scrotum = "cool storage for sperm production."**

## ELI-10 Explains

### Simple idea
The male reproductive system makes sperm and the hormone testosterone, and it has a set of tubes and glands that prepare and deliver the sperm.

### Analogy
Think of it like a specialized factory with a delivery route. The **testes** are the factories that make two products: tiny swimmers (**sperm**) and a powerful chemical messenger (**testosterone**). The sperm aren't ready right away — they first spend time in a "training and storage" area (the **epididymis**) to mature. When it's time, they travel through a delivery tube (the **ductus deferens**), pick up nourishing fluids from **glands** along the way (making **semen**), and exit through the shared exit pipe (the **urethra**). The whole factory is kept slightly cooler than the rest of the body (in the **scrotum**) because sperm production doesn't work well when it's too warm.

### What is actually happening
**Testosterone** is the hormone that, at puberty, brings the deeper voice, facial hair, and muscle growth, and it keeps sperm production going — all controlled by "boss" hormones (**LH** and **FSH**) from the pituitary, just like other glands. Each sperm carries only **half** a set of genetic instructions (**23 chromosomes**), so that when it meets an egg (which also has half), they combine to make a complete set of 46. Understanding this system helps explain **fertility** issues and common conditions like an enlarged **prostate**, which sits around the urethra and can make urination difficult.

### Where the analogy stops
A factory makes a fixed number of items, but the testes churn out enormous numbers of sperm continuously, day after day, from puberty onward — far more than any single delivery uses.

## Quick Recap

- The **testes** produce **sperm** and **testosterone**; the **scrotum** keeps them cool for sperm production.
- Sperm path: **testes → epididymis (mature/store) → ductus deferens → urethra** (as **semen**, with fluids from accessory glands).
- **Spermatogenesis** uses meiosis to make sperm with **23 chromosomes**; **testosterone** drives male characteristics, sperm production, and libido, regulated by pituitary **LH/FSH**.
- Relevant to infertility, low testosterone, and prostate conditions.

- U.S. National Library of Medicine, MedlinePlus — Men's Health topics (male reproductive health). https://medlineplus.gov/menshealth.html
